transcript:
This message comes from Angie. Angie has been helping homeowners find skilled pros
to get their home projects done well for over 30 years. For everything from minor repairs
to major remodels, find reviews, pricing, and booking at Angie.com or on the Angie app.
This is NPR News Now. The latest headlines every hour.
Live from NPR News in Washington, I'm Winsor Johnston. President Trump rallied supporters
in Georgia last night as he stepped up his campaign for Republicans ahead of next week's
midterm elections. Raul Valley, a member station, WABE reports on the promises and warnings Trump
delivered to a crowd in the city of Perry. Trump told his supporters that high oil prices will drop
dramatically after the Iran war ends and then added this. Our country is making hundreds of
billions of dollars because of what's happened in the Middle East because they're coming to Texas
and they're coming to Oklahoma and they're coming to Louisiana and they're taking that oil. Trump
also talked about sending federal resources to states represented by those he likes and backs.
Trump was more explicit in promising $5,000 for every adult if Republicans retained control
of Congress. For NPR News, I'm Raul Valley in Perry, Georgia. Former President Barack Obama
rallied Democrats in Michigan yesterday speaking to a crowd in Detroit. Obama said he sees voters
eager for change. People are so ready for something new, so hungry for something better,
so sick and tired of being sick and tired that everywhere you go it feels like change is in the
air. In Michigan, that's what I'm feeling right now. The rally came as early voting is underway
across the state. Voters in New York City are also casting their ballots early.
President Roderick Covington says there's a lot at stake heading into the election.
This is when it actually matters because this is the local election. This is where
it affects our neighborhoods, our streets, our subway systems, the city of New York.
Early voting has started in a number of other states, including Georgia and North Carolina,
with election day a little more than a week away. Researchers are now documenting the deadly toll
of this summer's extreme heat in Western Europe. NPR's Ava Berger reports on new findings about
the loss of life. 50,000. That's how many people researchers estimate died in Europe this summer
due to the sweltering heat. It marked the highest number of heat related deaths ever recorded for
the region. Researchers say climate change made that number so high. Two new papers from London
looked at hundreds of urban areas across Europe. They found that temperatures on the continent this
summer were 4.5 degrees Fahrenheit hotter than they would have been without climate change.
That may not sound like much, but they found that additional heat likely drove 60 percent
of those heat related deaths. The majority of the deaths were among the elderly.
Ava Berger, NPR News. This is NPR.
For more than a month, a large gray shark has captured the attention of people in South Korea.
NPR's Anthony Kuhn reports authorities have tried repeatedly, but unsuccessfully,
to coax the shark out of a canal in a city park. The 11-and-a-half-foot-long shark is named
Bukhangi after the North Port Park in the city of Busan, where he's attracted over 1.7 million
visitors since September 19th. Busan city government even appointed Bukhangi as its
honorary ambassador. After a third attempt to herd Bukhangi out to sea, the shark disappeared
on Friday morning. South Korean media report he was sighted again on Saturday near a port
passenger terminal about a mile from the canal. Authorities say Bukhangi appears to be in good
health and they hope he's transitioning out of the canal towards the sea. Some observers,
though, are worried that Bukhangi had to dive out of sight to dodge an oil slick on the water's
surface. Anthony Kuhn in PR News sold. Voters in Brazil are heading to the polls today in a closely
contested presidential run-off. Leftist president Lula da Silva is facing right-wing senator Flavio
Bolsonaro, the son of former president Jair Bolsonaro. The latest polls show the candidates
running about even. Bolsonaro finished ahead in the first round, but Lula has narrowed the gap.
High living costs and crime have been central issues in the campaign. Bolsonaro has promised
tougher crime policies and pledged to free his father, convicted of plotting a coup after losing
the last presidential election. I'm Windsor Johnston, NPR News, in Washington.
This message comes from U.S. Bank. Chief Product Officer Shruti Patel shares why U.S. Bank business
essentials is designed to bring together the key products small business owners need. Some of our
small business owners were telling us how complicated it was, having checking in one place,
will pay in another. And so our goal was to help business owners bring it all together by building
business essentials. This was really to help business owners focus more on growing their business.
Learn more at usbank.com/business. Member FDIC.

topics.text: President Trump rallies Georgia supporters in Perry, promising oil price drop and $5,000 payments
Former President Obama rallies Democrats in Detroit as Michigan early voting gets underway
New York City voters cast early ballots, citing local stakes in upcoming election
Researchers estimate 50,000 died from Western Europe's summer heat; climate change blamed
Gray shark nicknamed Bukhangi vanishes from Busan canal, reportedly sighted near port
Brazil holds presidential runoff between Lula da Silva and Flavio Bolsonaro, polls close
